quiz.question: How has the risk of dying in a plane crash changed over the past 50 years?

headline: Flying Is Now So Safe That the Statistics Have Essentially Run Out of Things to Count
teaser: You are sitting in an aluminium tube, seven miles above the Earth, hurtling through the atmosphere at five hundred miles per hour. Your brain knows this is fine. Your amygdala has reservations. The question of how safe commercial flying actually is has a curious property: nearly everyone knows it has gotten safer, but almost nobody guesses the scale of the improvement correctly. The number most people reach for would have been a reasonable answer decades ago, which is another way of saying their risk assessment is running on software that hasn't been updated since before the internet existed. The actual improvement in aviation safety over the past fifty years is the kind of number that makes you blink and then read it again.
metaDescription: 55% of people underestimate how safe flying has become. Fatal accident rates dropped from ~5 per million flights in the 1970s to ~0.07 today — a hundredfold improvement that nobody feels in their gut.
summary: In the 1970s, roughly five out of every million commercial flights ended in a fatal accident. Today that number is approximately 0.07. This means flying has become not merely safer but approximately a hundred times safer — an improvement so large that it has effectively outrun the human ability to intuitively grasp probability. Your brain, which evolved to assess risk by remembering vivid stories rather than consulting actuarial tables, remains stubbornly unimpressed.
nuance: The global average conceals real disparities. Airlines in North America, Europe, and East Asia have safety records several times better than the global mean. Some regions still operate with older fleets, less rigorous maintenance regimes, and weaker regulatory oversight. The improvement is also partly a story of survivorship — airlines with poor safety records tend to go out of business, one way or another.
brysonAside: The truly maddening thing about aviation safety is that the better it gets, the more terrified people become of the vanishingly rare exceptions. A person who happily drives to the airport through statistically murderous traffic will then grip the armrest during mild turbulence with the quiet conviction that physics has finally decided to stop working.

emailDigestLine: Commercial flying is now approximately a hundred times safer than it was in the 1970s, which is the kind of improvement your nervous system will never believe.
premiumTeaser: How did aviation become so extraordinarily safe? The answer involves a Swiss cheese model, a culture of blame-free reporting that most industries still cannot bring themselves to adopt, and the uncomfortable realization that the single biggest safety improvement came not from better engines but from teaching pilots to talk to each other.
b2bClassroomNote: Classroom discussion: Ask students to rank common risks (driving, flying, cycling) before revealing data. Connects to risk perception psychology and the availability heuristic. Useful for statistics and media literacy courses.
publishingNote: ASN and IATA data are consistent. The hundredfold improvement is well-supported. Strong shareability due to widespread fear-of-flying misconception.
